I was unable to search for Catholic/Orthodox sources, the NET Bible notes, or tradition-specific Lutheran/Wesleyan/Pentecostal commentaries due to tool limits. Below are my verse-by-verse notes.

## ZECHARIAH 3 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### Verse 1

**Traditional Reading**

- **Joshua the high priest** was the historical high priest of the post-exilic community (Haggai 1:1), one who returned from Babylon to rebuild the temple. In the vision he represents not merely himself but the entire priestly nation — he stands as a representative figure laden with both his own sins and those of the whole people (Ellicott).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

- **“Standing before the Angel of the LORD”** conveys priestly service, not mere spectatorship. Joshua was ministering in God’s presence. The "Angel of the LORD" here is understood by most traditional commentators to be a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ, since He is identified as Jehovah in v. 2 and acts as Advocate and Judge (JFB, Gill, Guzik).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm

- **Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him**: The right hand is the position of the prosecutor in a law court (cf. Psalm 109:6). The Hebrew *Satan* means "adversary." He is not Sanballat or a human enemy (as the medieval Jewish commentator Qimchi suggested) but the personal devil, the *διάβολος*, adversary of mankind (Ellicott, Gill).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-3.html

- **Reformed reading (Ligonier)**: Joshua represents the post-exilic community standing before the heavenly Judge, with Satan accusing him of sin and pointing out his unworthiness. The scene illustrates that God’s people have no claim on His favor apart from grace.
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/priest-filthy-garments

- **Baptist reading (Spurgeon)**: Spurgeon sees Joshua as a type of every believer: “We may very properly take Joshua as a type of all the people of God, as they stand in their sense of sin and natural faultiness, subject to the accusations of Satan, but delivered by their ever gracious Lord.”
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/zechariah-3.html

### Verse 2

**Traditional Reading**

- **“The LORD rebuke you, Satan!”**: The Angel of the LORD, who is Jehovah (JFB notes the identification), rebukes Satan directly. This is not a lengthy argument but a single, decisive plea: God’s electing choice. The rebuke is twice repeated for emphasis and certainty (JFB). Jude 9 shows Michael the archangel using the same phrase, modeling spiritual warfare fought in the LORD’s authority (Guzik).
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/

- **“The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem”**: God’s election is the conclusive answer to every accusation. If the issue rested on Jerusalem’s merit, condemnation would follow; but Jehovah’s choice rebuts Satan’s charge (JFB, Ellicott). This echoes Romans 8:33: “Who shall bring any charge against God’s elect?”
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm

- **“Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?”**: A “brand” is a charred, smoking piece of wood rescued from a fire — worth little, blackened, and about to be consumed. It represents Joshua (and the nation) as rescued from the Babylonian captivity, and more broadly the sinner rescued from deserved judgment (Gill, Guzik). The image emphasizes helplessness: the brand can do nothing for itself (Precept Austin).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-3.html
  — https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah_commentaries

- **Spurgeon’s threefold reading**: Spurgeon says this question bears three senses: (1) an exclamation of wonder — “Is not this a brand plucked out of the fire!”; (2) an inquiry of hope; (3) a defiance to throw in Satan’s face — “This one belongs to God by rescue.”
  — https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/gods-firebrands

- **Reformed (Ligonier)**: The Lord does not dispute the people’s sin, but rebukes Satan for bringing a charge against those whom God alone rescued from the fire. This is a picture of justification — God and God alone removes guilt.
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/priest-filthy-garments

### Verse 3

**Traditional Reading**

- **“Filthy garments”**: The Hebrew word is “the strongest expression in the Hebrew language for filth of the most vile and loathsome character” (Feinberg, cited in Guzik). The garments symbolise the guilt and defilement of sin (cf. Isaiah 64:5–6). Gill notes Jewish writers interpreted this as the sin of Joshua’s children marrying foreign wives (Ezra 10:18), or his own sin, or sluggishness in rebuilding the temple. But the primary meaning is that Joshua represented the priesthood and nation, both defiled by sin (Gill, Pulpit, Ellicott).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-3.html
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/3-3.htm

- **“Stood before the angel”**: He stood as an accused person awaiting judgment, humbled under a sense of his iniquities (Gill). JFB adds that abject as he was, he was still before Jehovah’s eye — God graciously accepts His people’s services even when mixed with sin and infirmity.
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm

- Gill notes the possible Roman custom of accused persons appearing in sordid garments, though he acknowledges it is uncertain whether this practice obtained in Judea at the time.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/zechariah-3.html

### Verse 4

**Traditional Reading**

- **“Take away the filthy garments from him”**: This command is spoken by the Angel of the LORD to the attending angels (“those that stood before Him”). The removal of garments symbolises the removal of sin — not by washing but by total replacement. Christ does not patch up our old righteousness; He removes sin and replaces it with His own (Guzik).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/

- **“See, I have removed your iniquity from you”**: The Hebrew verb (*he‘ebir*, Hiphil of ‘*abar*) means “to cause to pass over” or “pass through,” which came to mean forgiveness and deliverance (Utley, Gill). The Angel speaks as one having authority to forgive sins — a mark of His divine identity (Gill).
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/zechariah-3.html

- **“I will clothe you with rich robes”** (or “change of raiment”): Joshua not only receives the removal of guilt but also a positive imputed righteousness. This clothing imagery runs from Genesis 3:21 (God clothing Adam and Eve) to Revelation 7:13–14 (the white robes of the saints) (Guzik). JFB calls these “festal robes of the high priest, most costly and gorgeous; symbol of Messiah’s imputed righteousness.”
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm

- Ellicott sees here an allusion to Isaiah 61:10: “He hath clothed me with garments of salvation, He hath covered me with the robe of righteousness.” He argues the word simply means clean garments in contrast to the filthy ones, not necessarily “festal” garments.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

- **Reformed (Ligonier)**: This is “an image ultimately of justification, that act whereby God and God alone removes the guilt of sin and clothes His people with pure garments, a righteousness not our own, making peace with us in Christ (Rom. 4:4–5; 5:1).” Matthew Henry is quoted: “Christ loathed the filthiness of Joshua’s garments, yet did not put him away, but put them away.”
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/priest-filthy-garments

### Verse 5

**Traditional Reading**

- **“And I said, Let them put a clean turban on his head”**: The “I” here is the prophet Zechariah, interjecting in the vision. JFB notes Zechariah does not command but prays — “Let them set,” not “Set.” Seeing the change of raiment, he asks for the crowning touch: the priestly turban (mitre). The turban bore a gold plate inscribed “HOLINESS TO THE LORD” (Exodus 28:36–38), signifying full restoration to priestly service (Guzik, JFB, Ellicott).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm

- Ellicott notes that the prophet’s request was justified by the concern that the garment-change might only signify removal of the high priest’s own guilt, not his full reinstatement. The granting of the request confirmed full restoration.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

- **“And the Angel of the LORD stood by”**: The Divine Angel had been sitting (the posture of a judge, cf. Daniel 7:9); now He “stands” to see that the prophet’s prayer is executed and to give the charge that follows (JFB). It shows His approval and oversight of the whole transaction (Guzik).
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm

### Verse 6

**Traditional Reading**

- **“Then the Angel of the LORD gave this charge (protested) to Joshua”**: JFB notes “protested” is a forensic term for a solemn affirmation, almost an oath (cf. Hebrews 6:17–18). God solemnly declares the purpose for which the priesthood is restored: His own glory in their obedience and pure worship.
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm

---

### Verse 7

**Traditional Reading**

- **“If you will walk in My ways and keep My instructions…”**: This is a conditional promise. The cleansing of vv. 4–5 is pure grace, but continued service and privilege depend on covenant faithfulness. “Walk in My ways” refers to personal holiness; “keep My charge” refers to the due discharge of official duties (Ellicott). Utley notes this is not salvation by works but the “conditional element of a daily covenant lifestyle faith” — biblical faith is a way of life, not a mere creed or ritual.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/zechariah-3.html

- **“Then you will govern My house and have charge of My courts”**: A promise that Joshua would continue as high priest, ruling over the temple and its services, and keeping away idolatry and ungodliness (Ellicott, JFB). Some take “house” metaphorically as “My people” (cf. Numbers 12:7; Hosea 8:1), others as the temple building itself.
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

- **“I will give you a place among these who are standing here”**: Free access among the attending angels — the privilege of walking in God’s heavenly court. JFB says this means the high priest is granted association with heavenly angels. Guzik connects this to the believer’s privilege in Hebrews 4:16: “Let us therefore come boldly to the throne of grace.”
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/

- **Reformed (Ligonier)**: The conditional “if” is not a contradiction of justification by faith alone, because God never justifies a person and then leaves it finally up to them to persevere. All whom the Lord justifies He also glorifies (Romans 8:29–30). Joshua will not finally transgress because God preserves His own.
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-servant-branch

### Verse 8

**Traditional Reading**

- **“Hear now, O high priest Joshua, you and your companions seated before you, who are indeed a sign”**: Joshua and his fellow priests are “men of wonder” (Hebrew, *’anshê môp̄ēt*), meaning they have a typical or symbolic character — they point beyond themselves to a greater reality (JFB). Ellicott renders it “men to whom signs are given” or “persons accustomed to interpret enigmatical sayings of prophets.”
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

- **“My Servant, the Branch”**: This is a Messianic title used in Isaiah 4:2, 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5, 33:15. “Branch” (Hebrew *Tsémach*) speaks of a shoot from the seemingly dead stump of David’s line — something tender and seemingly weak, yet full of life and fruitfulness. Jesus used the same image in John 15:5: “I am the vine, you are the branches” (Guzik). The LXX translates it as *ἀνατολήν* (“day-spring” or “sunrise”), which Luke 1:78 echoes.
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

- **Reformed (Ligonier)**: The vision moves from the nation’s cleansing by grace to the Agent of that cleansing. The Branch is “the final Davidic king, the Messiah promised to the nation of Israel,” the reality to whom Joshua pointed as a sign.
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-servant-branch

- JFB notes the reference cannot be to Zerubbabel (as Grotius thought), because Zerubbabel was already in office, whereas the Branch is presented as future.
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm

### Verse 9

**Traditional Reading**

- **“See the stone I have set before Joshua”**: If “Branch” seems weak, God adds the image of a stone — solid and strong. JFB sees the stone as Christ, the foundation-stone (cf. Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 28:16; 1 Peter 2:6–7). Ellicott, by contrast, takes “the stone” (singular used as a noun of multitude) as the material stones of the temple being rebuilt — the laying of them before Joshua representing the whole building project. Both interpretations have historic support.
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

- **“On that one stone are seven eyes”**: In ancient thought, eyes represented knowledge. The number seven speaks of perfection and fullness. Guzik sees this as the perfect, all-encompassing knowledge and wisdom of the Messiah. JFB notes Calvin’s view: the seven eyes are carved *on* the stone, representing Messiah’s own sevenfold fullness of grace and the gifts of the Spirit (Isaiah 11:2–3; Revelation 5:6), and His watchful providence for His Church. Ellicott sees the seven eyes as representing God’s all-embracing, special providence (cf. Zechariah 4:10, “the eyes of the LORD which run to and fro”).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

- **“I will engrave an inscription on it”**: The engraving suggests finishing, beautification, or identification. Some early Christians saw it as picturing Jesus’ wounds (Guzik). Ellicott takes it as putting the final stroke to the work of rebuilding the temple, as engraving puts the finishing touch on precious stones (cf. Exodus 28:36).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/

- **“I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day”**: This is the great Messianic promise. JFB sees a primary reference to the Day of Atonement celebrated after the temple’s completion (Leviticus 23:27), but antitypically pointing to Christ’s atonement offered “once for all” (Hebrews 10:10, 12, 14). Ellicott argues “one day” refers to the day the temple was completed and consecrated, not to Golgotha, because v. 10 (peace and prosperity) could not describe the day of crucifixion. The tension between these views is well recognised.
  — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/zechariah/3.htm
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

- **Reformed (Ligonier)**: Though Zechariah’s contemporaries could not grasp the full detail, this promise looked to the one who would accomplish justification — removing iniquity definitively through the Branch.
  — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-servant-branch

---

### Verse 10

**Traditional Reading**

- **“On that day … you will each invite your neighbor to sit under your own vine and fig tree”**: This is a proverbial expression for peace, security, and prosperity, drawn from 1 Kings 4:25 and Micah 4:4. It pictures a time when every man sits undisturbed on his own land, enjoying the fruit of his labor without fear of invasion. Guzik sees this as the peace that Messiah’s reign brings — partially now for believers, fully in the coming Kingdom. Ellicott notes that the prophecy was partially fulfilled in the restoration after the exile, but its complete fulfilment awaits the future when “all Israel shall be saved” (Romans 11:26).
  — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-3/
  — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/zechariah-3.html

## TRADITIONAL DIFFERENCES NOTED

**Reformed (Ligonier / Sproul)**: Strong emphasis on this vision as picturing *justification by faith alone* — God alone removes guilt and clothes with imputed righteousness. The conditional promise of v. 7 is held in tension with the perseverance of the saints: God never justifies those He will not also preserve to the end. Ligonier explicitly connects Zechariah 3:1–5 to Romans 8:33–34.
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/priest-filthy-garments
— https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/gods-servant-branch

**Baptist (Spurgeon)**: Spurgeon reads Joshua as a type of every believer. The emphasis falls on the rescue (“brand plucked from the fire”) and the complete, gracious nature of cleansing. Spurgeon stresses that Christ pleads *before* Satan can finish his accusation — the believer’s security rests entirely on the Advocate. He also makes much of the change of raiment as forgiveness *and* imputed righteousness, the joy of all believers.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/zechariah-3.html
— https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/gods-firebrands
